names.name: atomic
names.said: Always last on the heat list, and usually printed in red.

etymology.root: Ancient Greek átomos 'uncuttable' → Latin atomus → English atom → atomic; the wing sense borrows the bomb's connotation from the mid-20th century, not the physics
etymology.first_attested: 1989 as a business name: Adam Lippin opened Atomic Wings in New York City that year, by the company's own account of its thirtieth anniversary in 2019. That dates the word's use for a wing business, not its first use as a heat level, which this project could not date
etymology.note: *Inference —* the ladder needs a top rung that sounds like consequence rather than measurement. Mild, medium and hot describe; atomic threatens. That is why the next rung up is usually a repetition — triple atomic, atomic scorpion — rather than a new word.

text.what: Top of a house heat ladder, and a word that only means something inside one bar's list. Wingstop's own description of its Atomic flavour is "It's the hottest we've got. Find out for yourself" — Spice Level 5, the end of its scale. An atomic at one counter can be milder than a hot at another, because nothing standardises the rungs.
text.story:
The word carries a whole apparatus with it. Bars and restaurants make an extra-hot sauce specifically so there is something to fail at, and reward whoever finishes with a photograph on the wall or the website, a commemorative T-shirt, a free meal, or some combination.

Quaker Steak & Lube runs the form at its most elaborate: its Atomic Scorpion sauce is published at 800,000 Scoville heat units, entrants sign a standard waiver, silicone gloves stay on, no bathroom breaks, and the finishers get a free t-shirt and their names on a chalkboard. Drinks are allowed, and there is no clock.

*Inference —* the waiver is the point of the word. A signature turns an order into an event, and an event is what gets photographed, which is what the wall is for.
text.how: Ordered by someone else's dare, eaten with a dairy dip within reach — blue cheese or ranch, both of which cut capsaicin better than beer does. Kitchens usually serve it in a small count and usually will not sauce a whole basket.

kin.as: The New York chain that took the word for its name, in 1989.
Publishes the word at the top of its own five-level scale.
The rung below it on most chain lists — heat with a fruit to hide behind.
Heat built into the cooking fat rather than bolted on as a top rung.
The other place wings became a spectacle with a crowd and a prize.
The dip argument, which an atomic order settles by force.
